mechanism: Additive bleeding risk: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and irritate the stomach lining while warfarin reduces clotting.
description: Taking an NSAID such as ibuprofen together with warfarin raises the risk of stomach and intestinal bleeding, and can also push the INR higher.
management: Clinicians usually prefer acetaminophen (paracetamol) for pain in people on warfarin. If an NSAID is unavoidable, INR and bleeding signs are monitored closely. Do not change either medicine yourself.
source_name: FDA label for warfarin sodium (Drug Interactions section), openFDA

mechanism: Additive bleeding risk via platelet inhibition and gastric irritation.
description: Naproxen combined with warfarin increases the chance of gastrointestinal bleeding and bruising.
management: Discuss an alternative painkiller with the prescriber or pharmacist; watch for black stools, unusual bruising or prolonged bleeding.
source_name: FDA label for warfarin sodium, openFDA

mechanism: Two different anti-clotting mechanisms acting together (anticoagulant + antiplatelet).
description: Warfarin with aspirin substantially increases bleeding risk. Some people are prescribed this combination deliberately after certain heart procedures, with close monitoring.
management: Only continue if a clinician has specifically prescribed both. Report any bleeding, dark stools or severe headache promptly.
source_name: FDA label for warfarin sodium, openFDA

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and gut flora that produce vitamin K, raising warfarin levels.
description: Clarithromycin can raise the INR in people taking warfarin, increasing bleeding risk.
management: Prescribers often choose a different antibiotic or arrange extra INR checks during and after the course.
source_name: FDA label for clarithromycin (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin can inhibit warfarin metabolism and alter gut vitamin K production.
description: Ciprofloxacin may increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, raising INR and bleeding risk.
management: INR is usually checked more often while the antibiotic is taken.

mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme clearing S-warfarin.
description: This antibiotic combination can sharply increase warfarin levels and INR.
management: Often avoided in people on warfarin; if used, close INR monitoring is standard.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 metabolism of warfarin.
description: Fluconazole can markedly increase the INR of someone taking warfarin.
management: Dose adjustment and INR monitoring are decided by the prescriber.

mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9).
description: Metronidazole can increase warfarin's effect and bleeding risk.
management: Prescribers may reduce the warfarin dose and monitor INR.

mechanism: Rifampin is a strong enzyme inducer and speeds up warfarin clearance.
description: Rifampin can make warfarin much less effective, raising clot risk, and the effect persists for weeks after stopping.
management: Anticoagulation is re-checked and re-dosed by the prescriber whenever rifampin starts or stops.

mechanism: Ibuprofen competes with aspirin at the platelet COX-1 site and both irritate the stomach.
description: Regular ibuprofen can blunt the heart-protective antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin and adds stomach-bleeding risk.
management: Clinicians may advise spacing the doses or choosing a different painkiller.
source_name: FDA Drug Safety Communication on ibuprofen and aspirin

mechanism: Two antiplatelet agents acting together.
description: Dual antiplatelet therapy is often prescribed on purpose after a stent or heart attack, but it increases bleeding risk.
management: Continue only as prescribed; report bleeding or dark stools.

mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which is needed to activate clopidogrel.
description: Omeprazole may reduce the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel.
management: An alternative acid-reducing medicine such as pantoprazole is often preferred; this is a prescriber decision.
source_name: FDA label for clopidogrel (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Additive bleeding risk.
description: NSAIDs with clopidogrel increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
management: Ask about acetaminophen or gastric protection instead of self-medicating with NSAIDs.

mechanism: Anticoagulant plus platelet inhibition and gastric irritation.
description: NSAIDs taken with apixaban increase bleeding risk.
management: Discuss pain relief options with a pharmacist before using NSAIDs.

mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition raises apixaban exposure.
description: Clarithromycin can increase apixaban levels and bleeding risk.
management: The prescriber decides whether a dose change or a different antibiotic is needed.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition multiplies simvastatin blood levels.
description: This combination markedly raises the risk of muscle injury (myopathy) and rarely rhabdomyolysis.
management: Simvastatin is usually paused during a clarithromycin course. Report muscle pain, weakness or dark urine.

mechanism: Azole antifungals inhibit statin metabolism.
description: Fluconazole can raise simvastatin levels and muscle-injury risk.
management: Watch for muscle aches; the prescriber may adjust therapy.

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4, increasing simvastatin exposure.
description: Simvastatin doses are capped when verapamil is taken, because of muscle-injury risk.
management: Dose limits are set by the prescriber; report muscle symptoms.
source_name: FDA label for simvastatin (Dosage and Administration), openFDA

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition increases atorvastatin exposure.
description: Clarithromycin can raise atorvastatin levels, increasing muscle-injury risk.
management: Prescribers may lower the statin dose or pause it during the antibiotic course.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce kidney prostaglandins, blunting blood-pressure control and stressing the kidneys.
description: Regular NSAID use with an ACE inhibitor can raise blood pressure and reduce kidney function, especially with a diuretic as well.
management: Occasional short use is often acceptable; long-term use needs a clinician's review of kidney function.
source_name: FDA label for lisinopril (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Both raise serum potassium.
description: Combining an ACE inhibitor with a potassium-sparing diuretic can cause dangerously high potassium (hyperkalaemia), which affects heart rhythm.
management: This combination is used deliberately in heart failure, with regular potassium and kidney blood tests.

mechanism: Additive potassium retention and intake.
description: Potassium supplements with an ACE inhibitor can push potassium to unsafe levels.
management: Only take potassium supplements if specifically prescribed, with blood-test monitoring.

mechanism: Additive hyperkalaemia risk.
description: An ARB with a potassium-sparing diuretic increases the risk of high potassium.
management: Potassium and kidney function are monitored by the prescriber.

mechanism: NSAIDs blunt antihypertensive effect and can reduce kidney perfusion.
description: Regular NSAIDs with an ARB can raise blood pressure and affect the kidneys.
management: Review long-term NSAID use with a clinician.

mechanism: Additive hyperkalaemia risk.
description: Both medicines raise potassium; together the risk of hyperkalaemia increases.
management: Regular potassium monitoring as directed by the prescriber.

mechanism: Dehydration or reduced kidney function from a diuretic can raise metformin levels.
description: Diuretics can affect kidney function and fluid balance, which matters for metformin safety.
management: Kidney function is usually checked periodically; stay hydrated and follow prescriber advice during illness.
source_name: FDA label for metformin hydrochloride, openFDA

mechanism: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose, opposing metformin's effect.
description: A steroid course can push blood sugar up in someone treated for diabetes.
management: More frequent glucose monitoring is often advised during steroid courses.

mechanism: Two glucose-lowering medicines used together.
description: This is a common deliberate combination; the main consideration is low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) from the sulfonylurea component.
management: Learn hypoglycaemia symptoms and treatment; follow the prescriber's monitoring plan.

mechanism: Sulfonamide antibiotics can potentiate sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia (CYP2C9 inhibition).
description: This antibiotic can increase the blood-sugar-lowering effect of glipizide.
management: Monitor for hypoglycaemia symptoms during the antibiotic course.

mechanism: Both increase serotonin activity; tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold.
description: This pairing raises the risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, sweating, tremor, fast heartbeat, high temperature) and of seizures.
management: Report agitation, shivering, muscle twitching or confusion urgently. Any change is a prescriber decision.

mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect plus reduced seizure threshold.
description: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures.
management: Seek advice before combining; watch for the serotonin-syndrome symptoms listed in your report.

mechanism: Serotonergic additive effect; fluoxetine also inhibits CYP2D6 activation of tramadol.
description: Raised serotonin-syndrome and seizure risk, with less predictable pain relief.
management: Prescriber review is needed; do not adjust doses yourself.

mechanism: SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin; NSAIDs irritate the stomach lining.
description: SSRIs with NSAIDs increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
management: Stomach protection may be considered; report dark stools or stomach pain.
source_name: FDA label for sertraline (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Additive bleeding risk via platelet effects.
description: SSRIs with aspirin can increase bleeding risk, particularly in the stomach.
management: Discuss gastric protection with the prescriber if both are long-term.

mechanism: SSRIs affect platelet function and may alter warfarin levels.
description: Bleeding risk increases when an SSRI is combined with warfarin.
management: INR and bleeding signs are monitored.

mechanism: Additive central nervous system and respiratory depression.
description: Opioids with benzodiazepines can cause profound sedation, slowed breathing and death. This carries an FDA boxed warning.
management: Only use together if specifically prescribed; never add one to the other on your own.
source_name: FDA Boxed Warning: opioids with benzodiazepines

mechanism: Additive CNS and respiratory depression.
description: This combination can dangerously slow breathing and cause deep sedation (FDA boxed warning).
management: Strictly prescriber-directed; seek emergency help for very slow breathing or unresponsiveness.
source_name: FDA Boxed Warning: opioids with benzodiazepines

mechanism: Additive CNS and respiratory depression.
description: Opioid plus benzodiazepine increases the risk of severe sedation and breathing problems.
management: Only as prescribed, at the lowest effective doses.
source_name: FDA Boxed Warning: opioids with benzodiazepines

mechanism: Serotonergic additive effect and lowered seizure threshold.
description: Raised risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures.
management: Prescriber review; report tremor, agitation or confusion.

mechanism: Diuretic-induced low potassium increases digoxin toxicity risk.
description: Low potassium from furosemide makes digoxin side effects (nausea, visual changes, abnormal rhythm) more likely.
management: Potassium and digoxin levels are monitored; report nausea, vomiting or visual halos.
source_name: FDA label for digoxin (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Verapamil reduces digoxin clearance and both slow conduction through the AV node.
description: Digoxin levels can rise and the heart rate can slow excessively.
management: Dose reduction and monitoring are prescriber decisions.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein transport of digoxin.
description: Digoxin blood levels can rise sharply, risking toxicity.
management: Levels are checked; report nausea, confusion or visual changes.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance.
description: Ibuprofen can raise lithium levels into the toxic range.
management: Lithium levels are monitored closely; NSAIDs are usually avoided.
source_name: FDA label for lithium carbonate (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Thiazides reduce renal lithium excretion.
description: Lithium levels can rise, with risk of tremor, confusion and kidney effects.
management: Dose adjustment with level monitoring, directed by the prescriber.
source_name: FDA label for lithium carbonate, openFDA

mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce lithium clearance.
description: Lithium levels may rise when an ACE inhibitor is added.
management: Levels and symptoms are monitored.
source_name: FDA label for lithium carbonate, openFDA

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal methotrexate excretion.
description: NSAIDs can raise methotrexate levels, increasing bone-marrow, liver and kidney toxicity.
management: Avoid self-medicating with NSAIDs on methotrexate; report mouth ulcers, fever or unusual bruising.

mechanism: Both inhibit folate pathways; additive bone-marrow suppression.
description: This combination can cause severe low blood counts.
management: Usually avoided; any use requires close blood-count monitoring.

mechanism: Reported higher incidence of skin rash when taken together.
description: Rash has been reported more often when ampicillin or amoxicillin is given with allopurinol. It is not usually dangerous but should be reported.
management: Tell the prescriber about any new rash so true allergy can be ruled out.

mechanism: Reported higher incidence of skin rash when taken together.
description: Rash has been reported more often with this combination.
management: Report any new rash to the prescriber.

mechanism: Reduced stomach acid lowers levothyroxine absorption.
description: Acid-reducing medicines can make levothyroxine less effective.
management: Separating doses and periodic thyroid blood tests are common; follow the prescriber's instructions.
source_name: FDA label for levothyroxine sodium (Drug Interactions), openFDA

mechanism: Timing/absorption consideration rather than a direct interaction.
description: Levothyroxine absorption is affected by many foods and supplements; it is usually taken on an empty stomach, separated from other products.
management: Ask the pharmacist how to space your doses.
source_name: FDA label for levothyroxine sodium, openFDA

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 metabolism of theophylline.
description: Theophylline levels can rise, causing nausea, palpitations, tremor or seizures.
management: Levels are monitored or a different antibiotic chosen.

mechanism: Absorption/chelation timing consideration.
description: Some antibiotics and mineral products can reduce levothyroxine absorption if taken at the same time.
management: Separate the doses by several hours if advised by the pharmacist.
source_name: FDA label for levothyroxine sodium, openFDA

mechanism: Oesophageal irritation risk from both products.
description: Both can irritate the food pipe if taken without enough water or while lying down.
management: Take with a full glass of water and stay upright for about 30 minutes.

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition raises carbamazepine levels.
description: Carbamazepine toxicity (drowsiness, double vision, unsteadiness) becomes more likely.
management: Levels are monitored or a different antibiotic selected.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 metabolism of phenytoin.
description: Phenytoin levels can rise into the toxic range (unsteadiness, slurred speech, drowsiness).
management: Level monitoring and dose adjustment by the prescriber.

mechanism: Both cause vasodilation through the nitric-oxide pathway.
description: Taking a nitrate with sildenafil can cause a sudden, severe drop in blood pressure. This combination is contraindicated.
management: Never combine. Tell every prescriber about both. Seek urgent care for fainting or severe dizziness.

mechanism: Additive slowing of heart rate and AV conduction, plus reduced contractility.
description: Together they can cause marked bradycardia, heart block or low blood pressure.
management: Used only with careful monitoring; report dizziness, fainting or a very slow pulse.

mechanism: Beta blockade can oppose beta-2 agonist bronchodilation.
description: Non-selective or high-dose beta blockers may reduce the effect of reliever inhalers and can worsen asthma.
management: Asthma history should be flagged to the prescriber.
source_name: FDA label for metoprolol tartrate (Warnings), openFDA

mechanism: Non-selective beta blockade blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways.
description: Propranolol can trigger or worsen bronchospasm and blunt reliever inhalers in people with asthma.
management: Usually avoided in asthma; the prescriber chooses a cardioselective alternative if a beta blocker is needed.

mechanism: Additive gastric mucosal injury.
description: Steroids with NSAIDs increase the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding.
management: Stomach protection may be prescribed; report stomach pain or dark stools.

mechanism: Both can lower potassium.
description: Potassium may fall, causing cramps, weakness or rhythm problems.
management: Potassium is checked periodically.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce the diuretic and antihypertensive effect and add kidney stress.
description: NSAIDs can blunt furosemide's effect and affect kidney function.
management: Long-term NSAID use should be reviewed by a clinician.

mechanism: Additive potassium retention and intake.
description: Combining a potassium-sparing diuretic with potassium supplements risks dangerous hyperkalaemia.
management: Only together under explicit prescriber direction with blood tests.

mechanism: Both can prolong the QT interval on the ECG.
description: Combined QT prolongation slightly increases the risk of a dangerous heart rhythm, more so with existing heart disease or electrolyte problems.
management: Report fainting or palpitations; electrolytes may be checked.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation and serotonergic effect.
description: Together they may increase QT-prolongation risk.
management: Clinician review for people with heart rhythm concerns.

mechanism: Enzyme induction lowers statin exposure.
description: Rifampin can reduce atorvastatin's cholesterol-lowering effect.
management: Prescriber may adjust therapy or timing.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation; fluconazole also slows ondansetron metabolism.
description: QT-prolongation risk increases with this pairing.
management: Report palpitations or fainting; electrolytes may be monitored.

mechanism: Duplicate therapy: two NSAIDs with no added benefit.
description: Taking two NSAIDs together multiplies the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney injury without improving pain relief.
management: Use only one NSAID at a time unless a specialist directs otherwise.

mechanism: Duplicate NSAID therapy.
description: Two NSAIDs together increase gastrointestinal, kidney and cardiovascular risk.
management: Use a single NSAID; ask a pharmacist about hidden NSAIDs in combination products.
